headline_en: Former minister Imran Ahmad remanded for three days in human trafficking case
summary_en: A Dhaka court on 21 October 2024 allowed police to question former expatriates' welfare minister Imran Ahmad for three days in a Paltan police station case under the human trafficking law over the Malaysia labour syndicate. The remand petition says a 100-licence syndicate controlled worker sending to Malaysia, demanded BDT 150,000 per worker for visa processing against an agreed BDT 78,990, and that BDT 24,000 crore was laundered through the syndicate.

facts.statement: On Monday 21 October 2024 Magistrate Mehera Mahbub of the Dhaka Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) court allowed police to take former minister Imran Ahmad on three days' remand for questioning in a case filed at Paltan police station, Dhaka, under the Prevention of Human Trafficking Act; police had asked for 10 days and the defence had sought bail.
Dhaka Metropolitan Detective Branch police arrested former expatriates' welfare minister Imran Ahmad from Banani, Dhaka, on the night of Sunday 20 October 2024.

On 3 September 2024 a case was filed at Paltan police station against 103 people on charges of human trafficking through an organised syndicate, naming former minister Imran Ahmad, former secretary Ahmed Munirus Saleheen, former MP Lt Gen (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury (managing director of M International Limited, as printed), and former MP Benzir Ahmed (owner of Ahmed International). The complainant is Altab Khan, owner of Afia Overseas.

According to the police remand petition, when the Malaysian labour market opened on 1 October 2022 complainant Altab Khan obtained demand letters from Malaysian companies through his own licence, but Imran Ahmad and the ministry secretary told him the sending process had to be completed through the 100 licences belonging to their syndicate.
facts.source_in_article: police remand petition (investigating officer SI Nazmul Hasan, Paltan police station)

facts.statement: According to the remand petition, the syndicate demanded BDT 150,000 (1.5 lakh taka) per worker for visa processing, while the complainant pointed out that the amount to be charged for sending a worker under the Bangladesh-Malaysia government arrangement was BDT 78,990.
The amount agreed between the governments of Bangladesh and Malaysia to be charged for sending a worker to Malaysia is BDT 78,990, as cited by the complainant in the Paltan trafficking case.
facts.source_in_article: complainant Altab Khan, cited in police remand petition

facts.statement: The police remand petition states that BDT 24,000 crore was laundered through the Malaysia human trafficking syndicate, and that the complainant was threatened after objecting.
facts.source_in_article: investigating officer SI Nazmul Hasan, Paltan police station

facts.statement: The remand petition alleges that Imran Ahmad, the main accused, helped the trafficking ring by having his wife's elder brother's son open an app named 'Ami Probashi'.
The remand petition says Bangladesh has more than 2,000 recruiting agents in manpower export, and that the syndicate created discrimination among these businesses.

headline_en: Not just raising remittances: what else must be done
summary_en: An opinion column by two North South University researchers, written after the July-August 2024 uprising, asks the interim government to recognise expatriates' role, free those jailed abroad for protesting, cut migration costs, reform BAIRA and the recruiting-licence system, legalise sub-agents, expand technical training and reintegrate returnees. It gives few hard facts beyond the fall in July 2024 remittances and the Malaysia syndicate figure.

facts.statement: After protesters urged expatriates on social media to use remittances as a weapon during the July 2024 uprising, remittance inflow to Bangladesh was about 35 percent lower than in June, and foreign-exchange reserves in July fell by USD 1.3 billion from the previous month.

The columnists say Bangladeshi workers in Middle Eastern countries who joined protests in support of the 2024 uprising risked jail and life imprisonment under those countries' laws, and that expatriates in various countries were jailed and fined; they ask the Chief Adviser to negotiate their quick release and job security.
facts.source_in_article: columnists Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder and K M Noor-E-Jannat

facts.statement: The column says 1.5 crore (15 million) Bangladeshis are spread across different countries of the world.
Citing a Prothom Alo report, the column says four MPs of the previous government controlled the Malaysia migration market and that the syndicate did BDT 24,000 crore of business in a year and a half.

The column says Bangladesh has about 2,000 licensed recruiting agents, more than the overseas labour market warrants, and that one person often takes multiple licences in the names of children and other family members so they can keep operating if one licence is cancelled.

The columnists allege that corrupt government officials are often linked with recruiting agents and that many such officials hold shares in the agencies; they call for them to be identified and punished.

The columnists propose reforming BAIRA (Bangladesh Association of International Recruiting Agencies), following the Indian model, and creating a ranking system for recruiting agents with ranking points, service quality and agent profiles published openly on migration websites.
The columnists propose that middlemen (brokers) should not be eliminated but brought under a legal framework and recognised, allowed to work for a minimum fee, with area-based offices if needed.

The columnists propose prioritising technical education and training centres in recruiting workers, a job portal where migrants upload CVs showing technical training so foreign employers can find skilled workers, district-level job fairs for returnees, and low-interest loans (at most 2 percent) for returned migrants who want to invest in business.

The column says returning expatriates face harassment at embassies and airports, including lost luggage, not finding trolleys and the absence of a separate line, and that Bangladesh has no plan for reintegrating returned migrant workers into society.
The column says many Bangladeshis are serving jail terms abroad for entering those countries illegally, and asks that they be brought home quickly and given jobs.

key_quote_bn: দেখা গেছে, দেশে দুই হাজারের মতো লাইসেন্সধারী রিক্রুটিং এজেন্ট আছেন।

headline_en: Malaysia labour market: BDT 24,000 crore trade, ACC opens probe against four former MPs in the syndicate
summary_en: The Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) has begun investigating four former MPs whose recruiting agencies were part of the Malaysia labour-market syndicate. The ACC summary says about 450,000 workers were sent in a year and a half at an average cost of BDT 544,000 against a government maximum of BDT 78,990, producing BDT 24,000 crore in trade, with syndicate agencies collecting at least BDT 150,000 per worker as a 'syndicate fee'.

facts.statement: The Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC/Dudok) has begun investigating allegations against four former MPs who traded as part of the Malaysia labour-market syndicate; a three-member committee led by ACC deputy director Mohammad Nurul Huda will conduct the inquiry and the ACC has prepared a summary of the allegations.

The four former MPs in the Malaysia syndicate are Nizam Uddin Hazari, Lt Gen (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury, Benzir Ahmed and A H M Mustafa Kamal; two syndicate firms are in the names of former finance minister Mustafa Kamal's wife Kashmeri Kamal and daughter Nafisa Kamal. All have been in hiding since the fall of the Sheikh Hasina government on 5 August 2024; Mustafa Kamal is reported to be in Singapore.
The government-fixed maximum cost of sending a worker to Malaysia is BDT 78,990.
On average a Bangladeshi worker spent BDT 544,000 (5 lakh 44 thousand taka) to go to Malaysia, against the government maximum of BDT 78,990.

In a year and a half about 450,000 (four and a half lakh) workers were sent to Malaysia, generating BDT 24,000 crore of trade; BDT 20,000 crore was taken above the government-fixed fee, of which more than BDT 6,500 crore was 'syndicate fee'.

Agencies inside the Malaysia syndicate received at least BDT 150,000 (1.5 lakh taka) per worker as a 'syndicate fee' while sitting idle; the ACC says senior government officials of both Bangladesh and Malaysia are involved with the syndicate.
Fourteen countries including Bangladesh send workers to Malaysia, but no country other than Bangladesh has such a syndicate system.

Former Feni-2 MP Nizam Uddin Hazari took a recruiting licence for Snigdha Overseas Limited in December 2018; in the next three and a half years it sent only 100 workers abroad, but after joining the Malaysia syndicate about 8,000 workers went in his agency's name in a year and a half.

Former Feni-3 MP Lt Gen (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury set up Five M International in 2015; it is the top single sender of workers to Malaysia, having sent 8,592 workers to Malaysia against about 2,500 to the Middle East since its founding.

Ahmed International, owned by former Dhaka-20 MP Benzir Ahmed, is the fifth-highest sender to Malaysia with 7,849 workers; before the Malaysia market opened it had sent only 238 workers abroad. Benzir was president of BAIRA, the recruiting agencies' association, when the syndicate was formed.

Orbitals Enterprise (owned by Kashmeri Kamal, wife of former finance minister A H M Mustafa Kamal) and Orbitals International (owned by his daughter Nafisa Kamal) together sent 9,861 people to Malaysia; Mustafa Kamal was finance minister when the syndicate was formed.

Other agencies the ACC lists among those sending large numbers of workers to Malaysia through the syndicate include Oishi International, New Age International, Catharsis International, BNS Overseas Limited, PR Overseas, Sadia International, Imperial Overseas, BM Travels Limited and Ananya Apurba Recruiting Agency; Awami League leaders and city corporation councillors and many new firms are also among the senders.
Ruhul Amin alias Swapan, known as the ringleader of the Malaysia labour-market syndicate, is not separately named in the ACC summary.

headline_en: Recent human trafficking context: timely initiatives (roundtable)
summary_en: A Prothom Alo roundtable for World Day against Trafficking in Persons (30 July 2024) with Winrock, RMMRU, BRAC, ILO, Justice and Care and others. Speakers describe social-media-driven trafficking, false marriages, forced cyber-scamming, under-age girls sent with fake IDs, the Madaripur-Shariatpur-Faridpur route via Libya and Tunisia to Greece and Italy, and weak prosecution and Bangladesh-India cooperation.

facts.statement: Winrock's Dipta Rakshit said traffickers use social media to lure girls with promises of higher earnings into illegal business in big cities and across borders; Bangladeshi women are being trafficked abroad through false marriages to foreign nationals, and highly educated young men are trafficked from Bangladesh and forced into cyber scamming.
facts.source_in_article: Dipta Rakshit, country representative Bangladesh and project director Ashshash, Winrock International

facts.statement: About 700,000 people are displaced in Bangladesh every year by natural disasters linked to climate change, and this population is at risk of trafficking.
facts.source_in_article: Dipta Rakshit, citing the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre

facts.statement: RMMRU's C R Abrar said trafficking-like cases within labour migration (deception, unpaid labour, slave-like conditions, passport and visa held by others) are hard to prove as trafficking, and such cases are told to be tried under the 2013 migration law instead of the anti-trafficking law.
facts.source_in_article: C R Abrar, executive director, RMMRU

facts.statement: During Covid a group of more than 300 migrant workers returned from Vietnam and were kept detained in Bangladesh even after completing three rounds of quarantine; the matter was resolved through a High Court writ, and who was responsible is still not known, although they had gone abroad following all safe-migration procedures.
A trafficker known as 'TikTok Hridoy' claimed that he alone trafficked one thousand people to neighbouring India.
facts.source_in_article: A K M Masud Ali, executive director, INCIDIN Bangladesh

facts.statement: The Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012 was enacted following NGO advocacy; it provides for protection of trafficking witnesses, but this is not being done for reasons including staff shortage, and the law is not properly applied in all cases.
facts.source_in_article: Salma Ali, president, Bangladesh National Woman Lawyers' Association

facts.statement: In Bangladesh anti-trafficking work is the responsibility of the Ministry of Home Affairs (in India the women's ministry works on it); Salma Ali called for involving the Ministry of Women and Children Affairs and for a Bangladesh-India understanding on prevention, protection, legal process and repatriation.

In several cases 14-year-old girls were shown as 21 to 23 years old using false ID cards and trafficked with promises of jobs; many Bangladeshi girls trafficked to hotels in Middle Eastern countries and India are forced into illegal work.

Of the trafficking incidents Justice and Care recently learned of, 40 percent of victims were connected through a social platform such as Facebook or TikTok; people aged 12 to 35 are the ones who become trafficking victims.
facts.source_in_article: Tariqul Islam, country director, Justice and Care

facts.statement: Traffickers open WhatsApp with SIMs of other countries so they cannot be tracked, hide their digital footprint, and investigations stall; most cases arising from cyber-based trafficking are not filed under the human trafficking law.
Tariqul Islam said that to his knowledge Bangladesh and India have never jointly investigated a cross-border human trafficking case.

People from Madaripur, Shariatpur and Faridpur show a trend of being trafficked via Libya and Tunisia to Greece and Italy, with climate change one of the causes; people of the southern coastal areas are among the main targets of cross-border trafficking.
facts.source_in_article: Nasir Chowdhury, project director, B-PEMS Agrajatra (climate change) project, Winrock International

facts.statement: A recent BRAC study found that only 5 percent of ordinary people understand migration and trafficking as separate things; the rest do not realise they are being trafficked.
facts.source_in_article: Shariful Hasan, associate director, Migration Programme, BRAC

facts.statement: UNHCR says Bangladesh is among the main countries whose people try to enter Europe by sea across the Mediterranean; cross-border trafficking occurs Bangladesh-India and Bangladesh-Myanmar, and there are cases of girls being sold to other countries after being told they were going to the Middle East.

BRAC's Shariful Hasan said people going abroad keep everything secret on the broker's advice; they must be told not to do this and to tell others beforehand where they are going and why. He said social media is now the main hub of trafficking.
ILO's Rahnuma Salam Khan said ILO has supported the government since 2011; a law, a recruitment agency code of conduct and an agency classification exist but are not properly implemented.
facts.source_in_article: Rahnuma Salam Khan, national programme manager, ILO Bangladesh

facts.statement: ILO's Rahnuma Salam Khan said indicators of forced labour include being held by force and having one's passport taken so that one works out of fear; ILO has a fundamental convention on forced labour.
ILO data say 28 million people worldwide are in forced labour, of whom 6.3 million are victims of sexual abuse (as stated).

30 July is World Day against Trafficking in Persons; the 2024 theme was 'Leave no child behind in the fight against human trafficking'. Winrock International runs the 'Ashshash' project working with trafficking victims at field level.

headline_en: No respect for 'remittance fighters' at the country's airports
summary_en: A reader's letter from a Bangladeshi living in Doha, Qatar, complains that expatriate workers are harassed at Bangladesh's airports, passport offices, training centres and embassies, and that sending a dead worker's body home is costly and difficult. He asks for bodies to be repatriated free at state cost and for an expatriate protection law.

facts.statement: According to government information cited in the letter, about 10 lakh (1 million) people go abroad each year on legal work visas arranged officially to 172 countries; counting other kinds of visas, a total of 20 lakh Bangladeshi workers go abroad (as stated).
facts.source_in_article: letter writer Minhaj Bin Mahbub, citing government data

facts.statement: The letter writer says expatriates are routinely harassed by some officials at Bangladesh's airports: made to sit for hours in the name of checking the goods they bring, cash taken from them in the name of tips (bakshish), luggage thrown about, misbehaviour and even physical assault; valuable goods bought for family are stolen at the airports.
facts.source_in_article: letter writer Minhaj Bin Mahbub, expatriate in Doha, Qatar

facts.statement: The letter writer says complaints by expatriates about airport harassment have brought no remedy so far, and that expatriates also suffer at passport offices and training centres.
The letter writer says that at Bangladesh embassies abroad, unless one goes through a broker ring, a one-day job takes three months of visits.

The letter writer says far more bodies of dead Bangladeshi expatriates remain abroad than are returned home; sending a body home needs a large sum many families cannot pay, and in many Middle Eastern countries fellow expatriates have to collect donations to send a body home. Getting embassy help with a body also involves much suffering.
The letter writer says that if an expatriate who borrowed to go abroad dies before repaying, the family gets no help from the state in repaying the loan.

The letter writer demands that the bodies of Bangladeshis who die anywhere abroad be sent home free of cost at full state expense and responsibility, that an expatriate protection law be enacted if needed, that airport baggage be given maximum security, and that embassy staff be more sincere.

key_quote_bn: দূতাবাসেও দালাল চক্রকে না ধরলে এক দিনের কাজের জন্য তিন মাস ঘুরতে হয়।

headline_en: Russia to take Bangladeshi workers, highest salary BDT 66,000
summary_en: A BOESL recruitment notice (published 1 June 2024) for 80 male Bangladeshi shipbuilding workers for the Zvezda (printed 'Vezda') Shipbuilding Complex in Russia under government management. It lists posts, pay of BDT 54,000 to 66,000, contract terms, the BOESL service charge and other fees, the documents and the 4 June 2024 deadline.

facts.statement: Under government management, Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) is recruiting Bangladeshi male workers for the 'Vezda' (ভেযদা) Shipbuilding Complex in Russia; applications are online.
Russia will take a total of 80 Bangladeshi workers in this BOESL recruitment: 20 ship painters, 20 ship outfitting assemblers, 20 metal ship hull fitters and 20 ship pipe fitters.

Applicants for the BOESL Russia shipyard jobs must have at least six months' practical experience of the relevant work in the international shipbuilding industry in South Korea, Singapore or other countries, must be proficient in English (those proficient in Russian get priority) and must have skill in the relevant trade.

Pay in the BOESL Russia shipyard recruitment: ship painter BDT 54,000; ship outfitting assembler BDT 60,000; ship hull fitter and ship pipe fitter BDT 66,000 (the article gives the figures in taka and does not state the pay period).

Terms of the BOESL Russia shipyard jobs: one-year contract, renewable; three-month probation; the employer provides accommodation with necessary furniture and primary medical care; food is at the worker's own arrangement; the employer pays the air fare to join and the return air fare at the end of the job; other conditions follow Russian labour law.

Finally selected workers for the Russia shipyard must work in temperatures of minus 11 to minus 30 degrees Celsius for three to five months a year; the notice says those prone to cold or allergy should not apply.
Selected candidates for the Russia shipyard jobs must pay BOESL's fixed service charge of BDT 56,350, plus a medical fee of BDT 2,000, a visa stamping fee of BDT 10,200 and other incidental fees.
No fee of any kind has to be paid to BOESL until a worker is finally selected, and all fees and charges must be paid through a bank.

To apply for the BOESL Russia shipyard jobs, candidates apply through the registration link and pay a BDT 100 fee, collect the payment receipt, then apply through BOESL's link with one copy of a CV in English, experience certificate, training certificate, colour copy of passport, the fee receipt and other information. The deadline was 4 June 2024.

headline_en: More than 1.3 million workers went abroad but remittances did not rise: RMMRU
summary_en: RMMRU's annual report on labour migration in 2023, presented at the National Press Club on 31 January 2024, says a record of more than 1.3 million workers went abroad, up 13 percent, while remittances rose only 2.88 percent and women's migration fell 27 percent. It notes Malaysia's regularisation, Greece's regularisation registrations, Oman's visa suspension and Bahrain's stop on Bangladeshi workers.

facts.statement: More than 13 lakh (1.3 million) workers went abroad from Bangladesh in 2023, the highest in a single year in the country's history; overseas employment rose 13 percent over the previous year but remittances rose only 2.88 percent, which is no growth once inflation is considered.
The number of women workers going abroad from Bangladesh fell 27 percent in 2023 compared with the previous year, while male workers increased.

In 2023 the most Bangladeshi workers went to Saudi Arabia, as in the previous year, followed by Malaysia. Although the highest remittances come from Saudi Arabia every year, in 2023 the highest remittances came from the United Arab Emirates; RMMRU said more research is needed to explain why.
About 25 percent of workers who went abroad in 2023 were skilled, up from about 23 percent the year before; sending of low-skilled workers fell 23 percent from the previous year.
Bangladesh's overseas worker numbers rose 84 percent in 2022 compared with 2021; in the same period Nepal's rose 300 percent and Sri Lanka's more than 100 percent.
In 2023 Malaysia gave irregular workers an opportunity to regularise.
More than 10,000 workers registered in Greece's regularisation programme for Bangladeshi workers in 2023.
In 2023 Oman suspended issuing visas to Bangladeshi nationals.
In 2023 Bahrain stopped taking Bangladeshi workers (as stated in the RMMRU report).
RMMRU called the recognition of brokers as sub-agents in the migration law in 2023 a positive development.
RMMRU's report said the trend of human trafficking to various European countries continued in 2023 as before.

Asked why remittances were low, Tasneem Siddiqui said expatriates' trust in banks has fallen, many are returning without finding work (though no data on returnees is available), and many send money to villages through hundi so it is not counted as remittance.
facts.source_in_article: Tasneem Siddiqui, founding chair of RMMRU and chairperson, Department of Political Science, Dhaka University

facts.statement: RMMRU recommended declaring 2025 to 2035 a migration decade, a specific budget allocation for manifesto promises on migrants, quickly restoring the online complaint system that had long been in operation, restoring workers' trust in banks, and creating investment opportunities for short-term migrants.

National Human Rights Commission full-time member Md Selim Reza said quality migration is happening in Japan and Korea because it rests on a coordinated system between the two countries, and that strong diplomacy is needed to achieve this with other destination countries.
facts.source_in_article: Md Selim Reza, National Human Rights Commission

key_quote_bn: ওমানে বাংলাদেশি নাগরিকদের ভিসা প্রদান স্থগিত করা হয়েছে, বাহরাইনে বাংলাদেশি কর্মী নেওয়া বন্ধ করেছে।

headline_en: Ambassador urges migrant workers to acquire skills before coming to Saudi Arabia
summary_en: A press release on the National Expatriates Day 2023 event at the Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh. Ambassador Mohammad Javed Patwary urged workers to check the job and gain skills before coming to Saudi Arabia, and described the Skills Verification Programme agreement, Open University exams for workers, welfare grants, and two Saudi law firms hired to recover dues of deceased workers.

facts.statement: Bangladesh's ambassador to Saudi Arabia Mohammad Javed Patwary urged expatriates to find out about the job and acquire the necessary skill in the relevant occupation before coming to Saudi Arabia, saying skilled workers get respectable work and several times higher pay.
facts.source_in_article: Ambassador Mohammad Javed Patwary, Bangladesh Embassy, Riyadh (press release)

facts.statement: On 27 September 2022, mediated by the Bangladesh Embassy, the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET) and the Saudi government-approved Takamol for Business Services Company signed an agreement to implement the Skills Verification Programme (SVP); under it workers in 29 occupations can pass a test in Bangladesh, obtain a skill certificate issued by the Saudi government and work in Saudi Arabia at higher pay.

On the Bangladesh Embassy's initiative, workers in Saudi Arabia who could not finish their studies can sit SSC, HSC and degree examinations through the Open University to raise their educational qualifications.

The Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh has signed contracts with two Saudi law firms to recover unpaid wages and dues of Bangladeshis who died in Saudi Arabia; 'last December' (article published 2 January 2024) BDT 33 crore in dues of the families of 65 deceased Bangladeshis was recovered and sent to Bangladesh.

The government gives financial assistance for treatment of sick workers, repatriates the bodies of workers who die abroad, and gives the family of a deceased worker a financial grant of up to BDT 3 lakh (300,000).
An 'Expatriate Workers Insurance Scheme' (Probashi Kormi Bima Scheme) has been introduced to bring outbound workers under insurance cover.
Migrants sent USD 21.61 billion in remittances to Bangladesh in fiscal year 2022-23; USD 3.07 billion of it came from Saudi Arabia, which the press release gives as 16 percent of the total.

About 1 crore 25 lakh (12.5 million) Bangladeshi migrant workers are employed abroad, and about 24 lakh (2.4 million) Bangladeshi diaspora live permanently in Europe, the United States and other countries.

With Saudi Arabia chosen as host of World Expo 2030 and the FIFA World Cup 2034, large job opportunities for skilled workers have been created in construction, cleaning, maintenance, and tourism and hospitality.

National Expatriates Day was observed for the first time in 2023 on the initiative of the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment; 30 December has been declared National Expatriates Day each year.

The ambassador inaugurated a special service week at the Riyadh embassy for National Expatriates Day and asked expatriates to use the embassy's services for any problem in Saudi Arabia or in Bangladesh.

headline_en: Plan to give 3 percent remittance incentive on the Probashi Card: Nurul Haque
summary_en: At RMMRU's 30th anniversary event in Dhaka on 13 October 2026, State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare Md Nurul Haque said the government plans a 3 percent incentive on remittances sent legally by Probashi Card holders, against the current 2.5 percent. He also spoke of grading the roughly 3,000 recruiting agencies, a pilot of the card in four to five countries, and the RAISE project for workers who return within six months.

facts.statement: State Minister Md Nurul Haque said there is a plan to give a 3 percent incentive on remittances sent through legal channels by Probashi Card (expatriate card) holders; at present expatriates get a 2.5 percent incentive on remittances sent legally through banks.
facts.source_in_article: Md Nurul Haque, State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment

facts.statement: A pilot of the Probashi Card is running in four to five countries including Jordan, South Korea and some Middle Eastern countries; the plan is for the card to allow financial transactions and payments at home and abroad and to give priority and discounts for treatment at government and private hospitals.

Bangladesh has about 3,000 recruiting agencies; the State Minister said that if they are graded on quality and competence, at most 300 to 500 agencies may survive, which would make control and supervision easier.

Workers who come back to Bangladesh harmed for various reasons within six months of going abroad are being given support, training and rehabilitation through the ongoing 'RAISE' (রেস) project, supported by the World Bank and international donors.

The State Minister said steps are being taken to settle expatriates' land-related legal disputes quickly: the plan is to arrange, in discussion with the land and law ministries, resolution on a priority basis within seven days.

The State Minister acknowledged complaints of broker dominance and extra cost in getting passports, workers not getting the promised job abroad, not getting needed help from Bangladesh embassies, and airport mismanagement; he said the government has identified 11 areas for solving expatriates' problems.

There are about 110 training institutions under the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment; the training system is being realigned to the demand and curricula of different countries.

headline_en: One million returned migrants in 10 years, a big danger for the economy
summary_en: An opinion column by Dr Sudip Roy of Bangladesh Open University argues that unexpected, premature returns of migrant workers, about one million in ten years and rising after the Iran-United States war, threaten remittances. He blames deceptive agencies and brokers, fake documents and weak pre-clearance checks, and proposes a returnee database, stricter verification, counselling, insurance and upazila-level help desks.

facts.statement: The columnist says about 10 lakh (1 million) migrant workers were forced to return to Bangladesh unexpectedly in the last 10 years, and that the number has risen recently because of the Iran-United States war.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Sudip Roy, Bangladesh Open University

facts.statement: According to a 2025 estimate by BRAC Migration Programme, about 5 lakh (500,000) workers returned unexpectedly in the last six years; the columnist says the rate so far in 2026 is much higher.
The column states that six to seven lakh workers go abroad 'every month' (as printed), while a significant number return early as undocumented, jobless, abused or sick.

The columnist says thousands are cheated by profit-seeking agencies and brokers through false job promises, visas that do not match the job, false skill certificates, and going abroad without verifying the reality, ending in ruin and loss of life.

The columnist says forged documents, false declarations and false certificates by some workers have damaged Bangladesh's image; workers in the Middle East say Bangladeshi workers are not regarded highly, while workers from neighbouring countries get many jobs in the same destinations, and Nepal's rate of remittance received is higher than Bangladesh's.

The columnist says the inquiry and verification process before granting emigration clearance is in force but decisions are often taken laxly, with more weight given to the outgoing worker's own statement than to the reality in the destination; he says the worker's signed undertaking (muchleka) cannot make the worker solely responsible.

The columnist proposes a database of returned migrants (how they went, what work they did, skill gaps, sending agent and receiving agent or employer), noting the airport immigration authority is already working on this; stricter medical tests and an end to medical-test fraud; and exemplary action against dishonest agencies, brokers and trafficking rings.

The columnist says that under the 1990 Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families, destination countries and Bangladesh should hold case-by-case discussions before a worker is sent back to check whether the non-refoulement principle is being violated.

The columnist proposes mandatory mental-health counselling and insurance for returned migrant workers, district volunteer teams, emergency government-arranged jobs in private factories, housing projects near export processing zones (as in Indonesia), a separate reintegration office if needed (as in the Philippines), and at least one desk or focal point at upazila level for information and help.

The columnist urges diversifying into health care, caregiving for ageing populations in developed countries and nursing through bilateral agreements and targeted training; he notes the nurse-sending process has begun but is not getting a response.

The columnist says many institutions have hired staff to serve returned migrants but many returnees do not know of the services or how to obtain them, and many are unwilling to travel to district towns or distant offices; he suggests linking IOM with migrant resource centres to extend to divisional cities and using union parishads.

key_quote_bn: ব্র্যাক মাইগ্রেশন প্রোগ্রামের ২০২৫ সালের হিসাব অনুযায়ী, গত ছয় বছরে প্রায় পাঁচ লাখ কর্মী অপ্রত্যাশিতভাবে ফেরত এসেছেন।

headline_en: 'I just kept staring at the rice': the story of two Bangladeshis back from a Libyan detention camp
summary_en: Two Madaripur men, Moshiur Rahman and Sohel Mia, among 174 Bangladeshis flown home from Tripoli's Tajoura detention centre on 1 September 2026 with IOM help, describe paying brokers BDT 32 lakh and BDT 39 lakh for the Libya-Italy sea route. Both were caught by the Libyan army within about an hour of leaving Khoms and held 45 and 48 days in overcrowded conditions with beatings, little food and salty water.

facts.statement: On Tuesday 1 September 2026, 174 Bangladeshi nationals held in the Tajoura detention camp in Tripoli landed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, on a special Buraq Air flight with the help of the International Organization for Migration (IOM); the article gives the landing as 10 am.

Moshiur Rahman's route from Bangladesh towards Italy: left in December 2025, 12-hour transit in Malaysia, 2 days in Sri Lanka, 2-hour transit in Kuwait, then Egypt, where he stayed five months; a broker then took him to Al-Khoms on Libya's north-west Mediterranean coast, where he was kept about three months in a 'game house'. The journey lasted nine months in all.

Moshiur Rahman of Madaripur paid brokers BDT 32 lakh in stages while held in the 'game house' at Al-Khoms, Libya; the money was handed to the broker's local representative in Bangladesh, and his family borrowed it from relatives at high interest.

While migrants wait in Libya, brokers phone the family in Bangladesh with sudden threats that the migrant will be imprisoned or beaten, forcing the family to raise more money; payments are collected in Bangladesh by the broker's local representative.

The sea crossing from Libya is called the 'game'. Moshiur's wooden boat left Khoms with 30 Bangladeshis and 4 Egyptians and was caught by the Libyan army after half an hour; they were taken to the Tajoura Detention Center in Tripoli, where he was held 45 days.

Conditions in Tajoura Detention Center, Tripoli, as described by Moshiur Rahman: 500 people in a room with space for at most 200; Nigerian supervisors beat detainees daily with long pipes over small matters; one khubz (thick bread) at 10 am, pasta at 3 pm with one medium bowl shared by seven people, the same food again at night; no rice in 45 days; only salty tap water to drink.
IOM confirmed Moshiur Rahman's return on 23 August 2026; he boarded the plane at about 2 pm Libyan local time on Monday 31 August and landed in Dhaka on Tuesday morning.
Sohel Mia left home 14 months before September 2026 and travelled Bangladesh - Malaysia - Sri Lanka - Kuwait - Egypt - Libya, aiming for Italy.

Sohel Mia of Madaripur spent BDT 39 lakh in stages trying to reach Italy via Libya: BDT 17 lakh in the first instalment and later BDT 12 lakh to a broker, then a further BDT 10 lakh through another broker named Sumon to attempt a separate 'game'; his family sold ancestral land to raise the money.

Sohel Mia's fibre boat from Khoms was caught by the army within one to one and a half hours at sea; there was then an attempt to sell the group to other trafficking brokers, from whom release would have cost another BDT 10 to 12 lakh.

Sohel Mia's group begged the soldiers to send them to Tajoura rather than sell them, because IOM visits the Tajoura Detention Center and a chance to return home can arise from there; he spent 48 days there before returning.
Sohel Mia said Tajoura was stiflingly hot with very few fans for the number of people, and that he spent Eid-ul-Azha in the detention camp eating pasta as on any other day.

After the returnees landed, the police Criminal Investigation Department (CID) spoke with them and gave contact numbers for legal assistance so that action can be taken against brokers; IOM told them to stay in contact for any problem, and Sohel said IOM told them they would get some money.

Returnees from Libya arrived wearing navy-blue tracksuits and carrying a blue bag given by IOM; the two men took the Azmeri Glory bus from in front of the airport to Gulistan to catch a bus to Madaripur.

Moshiur Rahman called the route a trap: seeing someone earn a lakh taka a month in Italy makes people lose judgment, and only after leaving does one learn how hard the route is. Sohel Mia said he will never go abroad again and urged others not to make the same mistake; he feared media exposure would give the broker an excuse not to refund money.
facts.source_in_article: returnees Moshiur Rahman and Sohel Mia

facts.statement: Sohel Mia said most young men of his village (Tekerhat, Rajoir, Madaripur) used to cross the sea to Italy, Greece and Malta.

headline_en: 174 irregular Bangladeshis return home from Libya
summary_en: On Tuesday 1 September 2026, 174 irregular Bangladeshis held in Libya's Tajoura Detention Center who wished to return voluntarily were flown to Dhaka on a special Buraq Air flight arranged by the foreign ministry, the Bangladesh Embassy in Libya and the expatriates' welfare ministry with the Libyan government and IOM. Most had entered Libya through traffickers to reach Europe by sea, and many reported kidnapping, ransom demands and torture.

facts.statement: On Tuesday 1 September 2026, 174 irregular Bangladeshi nationals detained in Libya's Tajoura Detention Center who wished to return voluntarily were repatriated; they landed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport at 9:47 am on a special 'Buraq Air' flight.

The repatriation of the 174 Bangladeshis from Libya was arranged jointly by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Bangladesh Embassy in Libya and the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, with the cooperation of the Libyan government and the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

Most of the 174 Bangladeshis repatriated from Libya on 1 September 2026 had entered Libya at the instigation and with the help of human traffickers, intending to reach Europe illegally by sea; many alleged they were kidnapped, held for ransom and physically tortured at various times in Libya.
IOM gave each Bangladeshi returning from Libya travel costs, emergency food items, primary medical care and, where needed, temporary accommodation.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs asked the returnees from Libya to tell relatives and neighbours about their horrific experience, to raise awareness of the risks of irregular migration.

The foreign ministry, the Bangladesh Embassy in Tripoli, the expatriates' welfare ministry and IOM say they are working continuously to bring home other Bangladeshis held in various detention centres in Libya.

key_quote_bn: প্রত্যাবাসিত বাংলাদেশিদের অধিকাংশই সমুদ্রপথে অবৈধভাবে ইউরোপ পৌঁছানোর উদ্দেশ্যে মানব পাচারকারীদের প্ররোচনা ও সহায়তায় লিবিয়ায় প্রবেশ করেছিলেন বলে জানা গেছে।

headline_en: Illegal journey to Italy: family has had no trace of Sagar for 10 months
summary_en: Sagar Mia, 20, of Madaripur has been missing since November 2025 after brokers took him via Saudi Arabia and Egypt to Libya for a BDT 23 lakh 'direct to Italy' deal, then took a further BDT 9 lakh for his release from captivity. His mother has applied to the expatriates' welfare ministry and filed a case against five people in the Madaripur human trafficking tribunal, and says the brokers are threatening her to withdraw it.

facts.statement: In Madaripur a broker ring contracted to deliver Sagar Mia 'directly to Italy' for BDT 23 lakh; the family paid one third on 2 November 2025, and the next day, 3 November, he was flown to Saudi Arabia, kept there two days, then taken via Egypt to Libya, where the Bangladeshi broker ring put him in a detention house and then collected the full BDT 23 lakh from the family by saying he would be sent on to Italy.
facts.source_in_article: mother's written application and case petition

facts.statement: Route used by the Madaripur broker ring for Sagar Mia: Bangladesh by air to Saudi Arabia (two days), then via Egypt to Libya, then a boat from the Libyan coast across the Mediterranean towards Italy; he was put on a boat on the night of 15 November 2025 according to the case documents.
facts.source_in_article: mother's written application and case petition

facts.statement: After the boat left, the brokers told Sagar Mia's family it had been seized by Libyan 'terrorists' and demanded BDT 20 lakh for his release; he was tortured when the money was not paid. The family then paid BDT 9 lakh through another Bangladeshi broker, Golam Mawla (48), and since that payment the ring has given no trace of him.
facts.source_in_article: mother's written application and case petition

facts.statement: Sagar Mia's mother Belatunnesa says the brokers took BDT 32 lakh in stages (BDT 23 lakh for the Italy contract and BDT 9 lakh for release); the family has lost its land and homestead.

Sagar Mia has been missing since 13 November 2025 according to the family (the article separately says he was put on a boat on the night of 15 November); in 10 months the brokers have given only assurances.

On 4 January 2026 Sagar Mia's mother Belatunnesa filed a case against five people in the Human Trafficking Offences Suppression Tribunal at Madaripur court, and also made a written application to the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment seeking her son. Madaripur Sadar Model police station OC Abul Kalam Azad said the police will investigate, that one accused had been caught, and that action will be taken against the rest.
facts.source_in_article: OC Abul Kalam Azad, Madaripur Sadar Model police station; case documents

facts.statement: Local broker Namzul Bepari (নামজুল ব্যাপারী) of Saidarbali, Madaripur town, works for Golam Mawla, son of Ismail Bepari of Mirzarchar Sipaikandi, Shibchar upazila, described as an active member of a trafficking ring with at least 10 assistants across the district who collect money and lure villagers; there are several cases against Golam Mawla and his assistants but all remain at large. Namzul Bepari denies being a broker; Golam Mawla's phone was switched off.
Belatunnesa says that after filing the case she faces harassment and threats from the brokers to withdraw it and cannot afford to run the case.

headline_en: National aspirations can be met by turning human resources into strength to build a prosperous Bangladesh
summary_en: An opinion piece by a deputy managing director of Dhaka Bank PLC on Bangladesh's demographic dividend, skills, freelancing and start-up finance. One section argues for changing overseas employment policy: aligning BMET training with international certifications, compulsory language preparation, collateral-free digital migration loans from Probashi Kallyan Bank and more government-to-government sending through BOESL.

facts.statement: The writer says Bangladeshis working abroad send more than USD 30 billion a year in remittances, yet most young migrants still go as low-skilled workers and face high costs, risk of death and uncertainty because of a broker-dependent migration system.
facts.source_in_article: opinion writer, deputy managing director, Dhaka Bank PLC

facts.statement: The writer proposes that the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET) build a skills framework aligned with international standards such as Japan's Specified Skilled Worker certification and Germany's Dual Vocational Training model, and that language preparation be made compulsory for overseas employment.

The writer proposes that Probashi Kallyan Bank introduce fast, digital, collateral-free migration loans based on verified employment contracts, and that government-to-government (G2G) sending through Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) be increased to reduce dependence on brokers.

General (not migrant-specific) enterprise finance in Bangladesh listed by the writer: Bangladesh Bank's New Entrepreneurs Refinance Scheme gives CMSMEs collateral-free working capital and term loans of up to BDT 30 lakh at a maximum 7 percent interest; the Women Entrepreneur Refinance Fund offers up to BDT 25 lakh on personal guarantee to women unable to give collateral and up to BDT 1 crore to growing small entrepreneurs at 5 percent interest; Karmasangsthan Bank gives micro-loans of up to BDT 75 lakh (as printed); Startup Bangladesh Limited runs a BDT 500 crore equity fund financing BDT 25 lakh to BDT 5 crore.

key_quote_bn: পাশাপাশি প্রবাসী কল্যাণ ব্যাংককে যাচাইকৃত কর্মচুক্তির ভিত্তিতে দ্রুত, ডিজিটাল ও জামানতবিহীন অভিবাসন ঋণ চালু করতে হবে।

headline_en: 10 Bangladeshis killed in factory fire in Saudi Arabia, all from Naogaon
summary_en: A fire on Sunday 9 August 2026 at a sofa factory in the Manfuha area of Riyadh killed 10 Bangladeshi workers, all residents of Atrai upazila, Naogaon, according to the headline, the list of names and the district's deputy commissioner; the upazila administration and the minister's condolence message speak of seven Atrai workers. The expatriates' welfare minister ordered quick repatriation of the bodies and government support and compensation for the families.

facts.statement: A fire that broke out at midday on Sunday 9 August 2026 at a sofa-making factory in the Manfuha area of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, killed 10 Bangladeshi workers, all residents of Atrai upazila, Naogaon; the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment confirmed the fire that night and Naogaon deputy commissioner Mohammad Saiful Islam confirmed 10 deaths.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare; Naogaon DC Mohammad Saiful Islam

facts.statement: The article is inconsistent on the toll from Atrai: it names 10 dead and says all are from Atrai, but also says the upazila administration, citing families, counted seven Atrai expatriates among the dead, and the minister's condolence message refers to 7 workers from Atrai. Atrai UNO Md Moniruzzaman said the death toll could rise.
facts.source_in_article: upazila administration; UNO Md Moniruzzaman; minister's message

facts.statement: The dead named in the Riyadh sofa factory fire are: Sagar (31) and Mojidul (34) of Bisha village, Bisha union; Farid Sheikh (32) of Udanpoi village; Sumon (35) and Hasibul Hasan (27) of Dubai village; Mohun Pramanik (42), Sumon Pramanik, Rubel Hossain (30) and Koli Pramanik (35) of Gondogohali village, Kalikapur union; and Abdul Jalil (38) of Parkasunda village, all in Atrai upazila, Naogaon.

Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said the Bangladesh Embassy in Saudi Arabia is in constant contact with the site and local authorities, and that officials have been instructed to bring the bodies home quickly and ensure all necessary government assistance and compensation for the families.

headline_en: Eyes now on two S Alam-linked hotels in Malaysia as investigations widen across countries
summary_en: A long report, drawing on Malaysia's The Edge, about investigations into businessman S Alam's overseas assets, including two Kuala Lumpur hotels; most of it concerns alleged money laundering and is not about migration. It also covers Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's planned visit to Kuala Lumpur on 21-22 June 2026, where reopening the Malaysian labour market, closed to Bangladeshi workers since 2024, is a priority, and describes the recruitment system, costs and the proposed 'Turap' system.

facts.statement: Malaysia's labour market for Bangladeshi workers has been closed since 2024 following many allegations, including conditions like modern-day debt bondage; as of June 2026 reopening it is a key priority of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's planned visit to Kuala Lumpur.
The problem peaked in 2023, when many Bangladeshi workers spent up to USD 6,600 each (about BDT 8 lakh, as printed) to reach Malaysia and then found that the jobs promised by employers did not exist.

When Malaysia stopped the entry of workers in early 2024, about 18,000 workers who had already paid agents in Bangladesh could not enter Malaysia; many of those agents have gone into hiding during the crackdown begun under the new government.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's first foreign visit is to be a two-day visit to Kuala Lumpur on 21 and 22 June 2026, with a bilateral meeting with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim on the second day; migration, the labour market, trade, investment and education cooperation are expected to be discussed, though the agenda was not final. The Bangladesh High Commission opened formal talks with Malaysia's foreign ministry on 24 May and Anwar Ibrahim confirmed the invitation on 1 June.

Bangladesh is reported to be considering including 432 recruiting agencies in Malaysia recruitment in place of the current 102 approved firms; a manpower-sector executive told The Edge that Bangladesh does not want the current method to continue and wants Malaysia to open recruitment to more Bangladeshi companies rather than a few chosen by some influential people.
facts.source_in_article: manpower-sector executive quoted by The Edge; reporter

facts.statement: The current 102 Bangladeshi firms are approved under the Foreign Worker Centralized Management System, built by Bestinet Sdn Bhd. Bestinet's founder Aminul Islam Abdul Nor is Bangladeshi by birth and now a Malaysian citizen; in 2024, after the fall of the Sheikh Hasina government, Bangladesh sought the extradition of Aminul and his associate Ruhul Amin, a matter still under discussion between the two governments.

Malaysia officially follows an 'employer pays' policy for recruitment costs, but effective implementation remains difficult under the current system; money changing hands in the Bangladeshi worker recruitment market reaches several hundred crore ringgit while the real recruitment cost is far lower.

Malaysia's Human Resources Minister Ramanan Ramakrishnan has proposed a new system called 'Turap' to stop exploitation of Bangladeshi workers at village level; Turap is also built by Bestinet, and some stakeholders in Bangladesh and Malaysia suspect it will again concentrate recruitment in a few firms.
More than 10,000 Bangladeshi students are currently studying at universities in Malaysia.
The report says the hidden agents were part of an arrangement under the Sheikh Hasina government in which politicians and recruiting agents worked together to benefit from Bangladesh's labour export.
